QF.id: AIFM CII AIFs in India and Suitability_3

question.text: At Saraswati Growth Fund, a new fund manager is debating whether a proposed pure private-equity buyout fund that targets later-stage profitable companies qualifies for Category I or Category II registration. Which of the following is the PRIMARY reason such a fund must register as Category II and not Category I?

answer.text: Category II AIFs are permitted to invest 25% in a single investee company, whereas Category I is capped at 10%
A pure Private Equity Fund is not in a sector that SEBI/GoI considers 'economically or socially desirable' and receives no specific concessions, so it is a residual Category II AIF
Category I AIFs must be open-ended, and a closed-end PE buyout fund is incompatible with that structure
Only Category II AIFs are permitted to invest in unlisted securities of investee companies

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 3, Category I is reserved for AIFs investing in start-ups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs, infrastructure or 'other sectors which the government or regulators consider as socially or economically desirable' — these receive special incentives or concessions. A pure PE buyout fund targeting later-stage scaled companies does NOT receive such concessions, so by exclusion it falls under Category II (which is defined as 'AIFs that do not fall in Category I and Category III'). The Trap: Option A swaps the concentration limits — both Cat I and Cat II have a 25% single-investee cap; 10% is the Cat III cap. Option C is backwards: Cat I AIFs are close-ended, not open-ended. Option D is false: both Cat I and Cat II invest primarily in unlisted securities. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A and XIX-C also test the Cat I 'concessions test'. XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) tests listed-market PMS which is structurally different from AIFs. Cat III (XIX-E) is the 'complex strategies + leverage' bucket and is not tested here. Manager's Pro-Tip: When a prospective Cat I applicant's strategy includes 'mature company buyouts', redirect the sponsor to Cat II registration during the pre-application stage — SEBI routinely rejects Cat I applications that cannot demonstrate the economic/social-benefit angle, wasting the Rs. 1 lakh-plus registration fee.
